product.title: Basque 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Basque (euskara): short dialogues, word-for-word translations that take apart every ending glued inside a word, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Basque is related to no other language on earth, yet much of it is friendlier than you'd expect: no masculine or feminine nouns, an article that simply sticks to the end of the word, perfectly regular spelling, and a verb that reliably comes last. Only two things are truly new: the doer marker -k, and auxiliary verbs that agree with who does it, what, and to whom — all at once.

blocks.text: Basque — *euskara* in its own name — is the only language in Western Europe that is related to no other language at all. It is not Latin, not Germanic, not Slavic, not Indo-European in any way. When the Romans reached the valleys on both sides of the Pyrenees two thousand years ago, this language was already there; every neighbor eventually switched to Latin and its descendants, but Basque did not. To this day nobody can say where it came from.

That sounds frightening. But "unrelated" does not mean "illogical", and English speakers are in for a pleasant surprise: much of what makes French, German, or Spanish heavy going — masculine and feminine nouns, an article standing in front of every noun, verbs that change shape for six different persons — is simply not here, or comes in a form that is far more regular than you'd expect.

Take the article. *Etxe* means "house". Add *-a* to the end and you get *etxea* — "the house", the one we already know about. English puts **the** in front; Basque bolts it onto the tail of the word: house → house**-the**. It feels odd for about a day, and after that it is completely regular.

Second, word order. The Basque verb comes at the end. *Nik ura edaten dut* — "I water drink". That is different from English, but different in an orderly, learnable way, just like Japanese or Turkish. Once your ear gets used to it, sentences become easy to predict: whatever matters most goes right before the verb.

What is truly new — and what makes this language famous among linguists — comes down to one thing: the doer marker. In "Jon comes", Jon has no ending. In "Jon**ek** bread eats", Jon gets the ending *-ek*, because in the second sentence he does something to something else. Basque marks *who acts on something*, not *who is the subject*. Linguists call it ergative. We'll call it the "doer's hat", and you'll be wearing it from Unit 5.

With it come the auxiliary verbs — *dut*, *duzu*, *du*, *zait*, *dizut* — short forms that pack three pieces of information at once: who does it, what it is done to, and to whom. A single word like *dizut* already means "I (do it) to you". This is the part that takes the most memorizing, so this course never dumps it on you at once: it arrives a little at a time, one small table per unit, always inside whole sentences you can use right away.

Basque is spoken by about 750,000 people in Euskal Herria — seven provinces in northern Spain and southwestern France: Bizkaia, Gipuzkoa, Araba, Nafarroa, Lapurdi, Nafarroa Beherea, and Zuberoa. The cities you'll meet often in this course are Bilbo (Bilbao), Donostia (San Sebastián), Gasteiz (Vitoria), Iruñea (Pamplona), and Baiona (Bayonne). The language taught here is *euskara batua*, the standard form used in schools, on television, and in books — understood across the whole region.

One more thing you should know from the start: in Euskal Herria, choosing to speak euskara means something. Nearly every speaker is also fluent in Spanish or French, so no one *has* to speak euskara with you. If you try — even just *kaixo* and *eskerrik asko* — the reaction is almost always surprisingly warm. The most useful sentence in this whole course may well be this one: *Euskara ikasten ari naiz* — "I'm learning Basque".

The twenty units ahead are meant to be worked through one at a time, about three or four days per unit. Don't memorize the tables first; read the dialogue aloud until it feels good in your mouth, then look at the explanations. This language isn't hard — you just haven't heard it before. *Ondo ibili!*

Every unit has the same layout, and there's a reason for it. You meet the language first as living sentences, and only then the explanation. Reversing that order — memorizing tables first — is the fastest way to make Basque feel impossible.
Set aside thirty to forty minutes a day. Four days in a row at half an hour each beats one long session once a week; Basque endings stick through repetition, not through hours at the desk.

items: **By the end of this unit** — three things you'll be able to do once the unit is done. Read them first, and again at the end as a self-check.

**Dialogue** — twelve lines of natural conversation. Each line has three layers: Basque, a natural translation, and a **literal** translation that takes every word apart (`house-in`, `I-have-it`). The literal layer is the main tool of this course.
**Dialogue notes** — four notes that answer the questions that just popped into your head while reading.
**Grammar sections** — two or three per unit, with tables and warning boxes for the mistakes English speakers typically make.
**Vocabulary** — the unit's thirty or so words, each with an English-friendly pronunciation guide.
**Exercises** — four sets, twenty-four items. Do them on paper, not in your head.
**Answer key** — on the following page. Check yourself, and if you got something wrong, find the dialogue line that contains the pattern.

blocks.title: How to read the literal translation
items: Hyphens join the pieces that are glued into one word in Basque. *Etxean* → `house-in`. *Dut* → `I-have-it`. *Zaizu* → `to-you-it`.
If one Basque word needs three English words, all three are joined: *dizut* → `I-to-you-it`.
The literal translation is deliberately awkward. If it read smoothly, it would fail to show how Basque builds its sentences.

blocks.title: If you only have ten minutes today
items: Read the dialogue aloud once, all the way through, without stopping at words you don't know.
Read it once more, following the literal layer.
Close the book. Tomorrow, start with the dialogue notes. Ten minutes actually done beats an hour that was only planned.

blocks.title: Tap to listen
items: If you're reading this course in the Library on your Linguo dashboard, you can tap any Basque word to hear it.
Use that above all for *tx*, *tz*, *ts*, and *x* — the four sounds that get mixed up most at the start, and that sort themselves out fastest once your ear has heard them.

blocks.text: Basque may be nobody's relative, but it has lived next door to Latin, Spanish, and French for two thousand years — and borrowed quietly. Many of those same Latin words also reached English, so you already know hundreds of Basque words before Unit 1 begins.
Old loans from Latin
International words — the same in both languages
And the other way round: Basque words that went out into the world

The traffic wasn't one-way. *Ezker* ("left") became *izquierda* in Spanish. *Bizar* ("beard") probably became *bizarre* in French and English — bearded men looked strange to clean-shaven neighbors. *Txatarra* ("scrap, junk") became Spanish *chatarra*. And the sport *jai alai* — literally "merry festival" — is used as is all over the world.

blocks.title: Careful: looking alike doesn't mean the same
items: *Gela* means "room" (from Latin *cella*, like English *cell*), not "gel". A drinking glass is *edalontzia*.
*Ura* means "water" — nothing to do with "your" or "you're". It is one of the most important words in the whole course.
*Bost* means "five", not "boss". *Bat* means "one", not a bat. And *bake* means "peace", not "bake".
*Ama* means "mother" and *aita* means "father" — *ama* looks like "mama", a happy coincidence, but only a coincidence.

blocks.text: Good news first: Basque is written exactly as it sounds, one letter, one sound, no surprises. There are five vowels — a, e, i, o, u — short and pure, as in Spanish or Italian. No long vowels, no nasal vowels, no German *ü*. The "Say it" column spells them **ah** (*father*), **eh** (*bed*), **ee** (*see*), **oh** (a pure o, with no "w" glide), **oo** (*food*); **g** is always hard as in *go*, and **kh** is the throaty sound in Scottish *loch*.

blocks.title: Four sounds that decide everything
items: *tx*, *tz*, *ts*, and *x* are the calling card of Basque. If you only have time to practice one thing from this page, practice these four.
Shortcut for English speakers: **tx = ch** (church), **tz = ts** (cats), **x = sh** (ship), **ts = a heavier ts**, made with the tongue tip against the ridge behind your teeth.
Test yourself with these four words: *txakurra* (dog), *hitza* (word), *hotsa* (sound), *xagua* (mouse).

blocks.text: Word stress

Basque has almost no stress that changes meaning. The general habit: the second syllable is a little stronger, and the last syllable drops slightly. Because stress never distinguishes words, stressing the wrong syllable never changes the meaning — a big relief compared with Spanish or English. The "Say it" column in this course still marks the slightly stronger syllable in capitals, as a guide to rhythm, not a hard rule.
Rare letters

The letters *c*, *q*, *v*, *w*, and *y* are practically absent from native Basque words; if you meet one, it is almost certainly a foreign name or a recent loan. On the other hand, *k* and *tz* are everywhere — and *k* is the letter that becomes the "doer's hat" in Unit 5.

One more: the letter *h*. In the south (Spain) it is not pronounced at all — *hemen* sounds like "EH-mehn", *hori* like "OH-ree". In the north (France) it is still heard as a soft breath. This course follows the southern usage of most speakers, so the "Say it" column always leaves the *h* out. But you still have to write it: *hori* (that) and *ori* are not the same word.

blocks.title: Typical mistakes of English speakers
items: Reading *z* like the English "z" in *zebra*. Basque has no such sound at all — *z* is always **s**.
Reading *j* like the English "j" in *jam*. *Jan* ("eat") sounds like "khahn", not "jan".
Swallowing *rr*. *Txakurra* (dog) and *txakura* are not the same sound to a native ear — roll the *rr*.
Pronouncing *h*. In the south *h* is completely silent; *hotela* sounds like "oh-TEH-lah".

blocks.text: Ten words to practice it all at once
Articles and plurals — endings that stick
A word that already ends in *-a* doesn't add another *-a*: *neska* (girl) → *neska*, plural *neskak*.
Cases — the most common endings
Personal pronouns
Three auxiliary patterns
Tenses used in this course
Building a sentence

items: The verb goes at the **end**: *Nik euskara ikasten dut*.
Whatever matters most goes **right before** the verb: *Nik EUSKARA ikasten dut* (what I'm learning is Basque).
Negate with *ez*, and the auxiliary jumps to the front: *Ez dut euskara ikasten*.
Yes/no questions need only a rising tone, or *al*: *Euskara ikasten **al** duzu?*
Adjectives come **after** the noun, and the article sticks to the adjective: *etxe **handia*** (the big house).

blocks.text: Numbers
These forty verbs cover nearly all everyday conversation at A1. The second column is the dictionary form (the participle); the third is the *-t(z)en* form used for habits and for "-ing".

blocks.title: NORK-NOR auxiliary (ukan) — learn this first
items: Singular object: **dut** (I), **duzu** (you), **du** (he/she), **dugu** (we), **duzue** (you all), **dute** (they).
Plural object: **ditut**, **dituzu**, **ditu**, **ditugu**, **dituzue**, **dituzte**.
Past: **nuen**, **zenuen**, **zuen**, **genuen**, **zenuten**, **zuten**.

blocks.title: NOR auxiliary (izan) — its partner
items: Present: **naiz**, **zara**, **da**, **gara**, **zarete**, **dira**.
Past: **nintzen**, **zinen**, **zen**, **ginen**, **zineten**, **ziren**.
*Egon* (to be located) stands on its own: **nago**, **zaude**, **dago**, **gaude**, **zaudete**, **daude**.

blocks.text: After these twenty units you can introduce yourself, order food, ask for directions, talk about yesterday, and plan a weekend — all in euskara, using the three most common auxiliary patterns. That is a full A1. What comes next isn't really new; it's an extension of what you already have.
What's waiting at A2

items: The full **NORK-NORI-NOR** auxiliary — *dizkiot*, *zenidan*, and the whole family.
**Hitanoa** (*duk*/*dun*), a very familiar form of address that differs for male and female listeners — the only place gender shows up in this language.
Subordinate clauses: *-ela* (that), *-enean* (when), *ba-* (if).
Commands and the conditional: *emadazu*, *joango nintzateke*.
**Synthetic** verbs — a handful of verbs that can stand without an auxiliary: *dakit*, *daramat*, *dabil*.

blocks.text: How to keep going without a teacher

items: **EITB** (eitb.eus) — Basque-language TV and radio, with children's shows that speak slowly and clearly.
**Elhuyar hiztegia** (hiztegiak.elhuyar.eus) — the most complete online dictionary, Basque–Spanish–English.
**Bertsolaritza** — improvised sung verse; listen once even if you don't understand yet, because this is the heart of Basque culture.
**Euskaltegi** — Basque language schools in every town in Euskal Herria; many offer online classes.
Watch Basque films with Basque subtitles, not English ones — your eyes and ears need to train on the same language.

blocks.text: And one last tip you won't find in any table: use it. Basque has survived two thousand years not because its grammar is tidy, but because people kept using it in the kitchen, at the market, and in the street. Every time you choose *eskerrik asko* over *gracias*, you become part of that. *Ondo ibili, eta zorte on!*
